Its entries pair promises with status labels, including “Kept,” “In progress” and “It’s complicated,” and identify a reported method such as an executive order or diplomacy. proposal.description_long: The Associated Press published a project to track selected promises Donald Trump made during his 2024 campaign. The archived version reviewed here presents commitments alongside a status and, for some entries, a reported method of action. Its labels include “Kept,” “In progress,” and “It’s complicated”; examples of methods shown in the table include executive action, an agency announcement, diplomacy, or congressional action. The project therefore offers a promise-by-promise tracking format, rather than a single verdict on the administration. The live AP page currently exposes only its title in the focused text retrieval, so the archived copy is the source for the visible classifications described here. Because this is a changing tracker, those labels should be tied to the dated archived view rather than treated as current indefinitely. The available evidence does not establish a March 4 snapshot, totals across policy areas, or that AP’s labels changed Trump’s public messaging. This draft removes those unsupported comparisons and describes only the tracker and the classifications visible in the cited capture.

proposal.title: UK Bill Proposed Police Powers to Restrict Protesters’ Face Coverings
proposal.description_short: A June 2025 report described proposed UK police powers to restrict face coverings at designated protests; it did not report a Trump administration policy.
proposal.description_medium: Byline Times reported on June 3, 2025 that the UK government’s proposed Crime and Policing Bill included police powers to restrict face coverings at protests. The article relayed human-rights groups’ concerns about effects on disabled people, Muslim women and dissidents. It described a proposal moving through Parliament, not an enacted U.S. rule or a Trump administration action.
proposal.description_long: The UK government’s February 2025 fact sheet for the Crime and Policing Bill described a proposed offence involving identity-concealing items in an area designated by police because of a risk of protest-related offending. During Commons committee debate on April 29, Home Office minister Diana Johnson said an inspector could designate a locality when the statutory conditions were met and that the offence would not apply at every protest. The committee record also describes defences for uses related to health, religious observance, or work. Byline Times reported on June 3 that the bill was being considered by Parliament and discussed possible facial-recognition access to DVLA images; that additional technology claim is not established by the cited official fact sheet or committee passage. The documented proposal was made by the UK government under Prime Minister Keir Starmer. None of the supplied reporting establishes a Trump administration mask ban, U.S. enforcement, or a connection to Donald Trump. The grounded draft therefore describes the UK bill as a proposal at the cited dates and recommends excluding it from a Trump-specific record.

proposal.description_long: A Senate committee investigated Federal Housing Administration programs in 1954, including apartment projects associated with Fred Trump and other developers. The supplied timeline reports that Trump and a partner received at least $3.5 million more than the complexes cost to build and that $16 million in FHA-backed financing was allocated across six Trump-owned properties. Those figures describe the allegation and financing discussed in the inquiry; they should not be presented as a final finding of unlawful conduct. The timeline says that the investigation found no law had been broken and that the FHA blacklisted Trump the following year. The cited Washington Post-hosted Senate interview is a primary source for his testimony, while the timeline is the source for the claimed later blacklist. The packet does not include an FHA order, agency record or committee document establishing that sanction. The revised title therefore identifies the Senate investigation and does not state that the FHA blacklisted him. A final committee report or contemporaneous FHA decision is needed to substantiate the claimed outcome. The available evidence also does not establish that the inquiry was connected to Donald Trump’s later political career.

proposal.title: FinCEN Assessed a $10 Million Penalty Against Trump Taj Mahal in 2015
proposal.description_short: FinCEN imposed a $10 million penalty for willful Bank Secrecy Act violations, including reporting and recordkeeping failures.
proposal.description_medium: FinCEN said in March 2015 that Trump Taj Mahal Casino Resort would pay a $10 million civil penalty for willful and repeated Bank Secrecy Act violations. The agency cited anti-money-laundering program, reporting, and recordkeeping failures, and noted an earlier $477,700 penalty in 1998 for currency-transaction-report violations. proposal.description_long: On March 6, 2015, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) announced a $10 million civil money penalty against Trump Taj Mahal Casino Resort for willful and repeated violations of the Bank Secrecy Act. FinCEN said the casino admitted to violations involving its anti-money-laundering program, reporting obligations, and recordkeeping requirements. The agency also described a history of prior compliance findings and referenced a $477,700 civil penalty it had assessed in 1998 for currency-transaction-reporting violations. The 2015 action therefore supports a specific regulatory enforcement account: the agency, amount, date, statute, and broad violation areas are identified. It does not, by itself, establish a criminal conviction, prove every transaction was unlawful, or support claims about political motive or wider significance. The previous packet lacked those enforcement details; FinCEN’s release and penalty assessment supply them. The title is narrowed to the documented 2015 penalty rather than making an unspecific “fined again” claim.

proposal.title: Eric Trump Predicts COVID-19 Would Vanish After the Election
proposal.description_short: On Fox News, Eric Trump said Democrats were exploiting the COVID-19 crisis and predicted it would disappear after the November election.
proposal.description_medium: Eric Trump told Jeanine Pirro on Fox News’s Justice with Judge Jeanine that Democrats were trying to exploit the COVID-19 crisis and predicted the coronavirus would “magically” disappear after November 3. Media Matters dates the recorded segment to May 16, 2020; Fox News published its report shortly after midnight May 17. This resolves the broadcast-versus-publication date discrepancy.
proposal.description_long: In a May 16, 2020 appearance on Fox News’s Justice with Judge Jeanine, Eric Trump said Democrats were trying to exploit the coronavirus crisis to damage his father’s reelection campaign. He predicted that after November 3 the coronavirus would “magically all of a sudden go away and disappear” and the country would reopen. Fox News published its report at 12:13 a.m. Eastern on May 17 and quotes the interview. Media Matters labels the video as the May 16 edition of the program, while the Washington Post also reported the comments on May 17. The dates refer to the broadcast and the following day’s publication, rather than conflicting event dates. The record can describe the remarks with attribution and distinguish the clip date from the article date. These sources document what Eric Trump said; they do not support presenting his claim about the virus or political motives as fact.

proposal.title: Brennan Center: Project 2025 Proposes Federal Intervention in Local Prosecutors’ Cases
proposal.description_short: The Brennan Center says Project 2025 proposes DOJ intervention in some local prosecutorial choices and efforts to end existing consent decrees.
proposal.description_medium: The Brennan Center’s January 2025 analysis says Project 2025 proposes that the Justice Department charge or intervene against elected local prosecutors over policies it labels “rule of law deficiencies,” including some decisions not to prosecute low-level offenses. The analysis also describes a proposal to eliminate existing DOJ consent decrees. It presents these as plan provisions and risks, not proof that every proposal was implemented.
proposal.description_long: A January 29, 2025 Brennan Center analysis describes criminal-justice proposals in Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation’s policy blueprint for a conservative administration. It says the plan would let the Justice Department charge or intervene against local prosecutors whose policies are labeled “rule of law deficiencies,” including some decisions not to prosecute low-level offenses such as marijuana or shoplifting cases. The analysis also says Project 2025 proposes eliminating existing DOJ consent decrees; it notes that nearly 30 such agreements then covered law-enforcement and jail systems. Consent decrees are court-approved agreements used to remedy unlawful practices, so the Center warns that removing them would reduce federal oversight of local agencies. These are provisions and risk assessments described by the Brennan Center, not proof that all proposals were implemented. The original description’s claims of a permanent constitutional restoration, arrests of opposition leaders, protest bans, revoked citizenship, and forced dissolution of organizations are not supported by the supplied links. The revised account sticks to specific policy proposals and attributes the projected effects to the analysis.

proposal.title: Senator Reports Whistleblower Allegations About FBI Aircraft and Kirk Probe
proposal.description_short: Senator Reports Whistleblower Allegations About FBI Aircraft and Kirk Probe
proposal.description_medium: A Senate Judiciary Committee release says Sen. Dick Durbin disclosed whistleblower information alleging that FBI Director Kash Patel’s aircraft decisions affected or delayed high-profile investigations, including the Charlie Kirk killing. Durbin said the FBI shooting-reconstruction team was asked to fly to Utah to process the scene. This is an account of whistleblower allegations by the committee’s ranking member, not an independent finding that a delay occurred or that personal travel caused it.
proposal.description_long: In a Senate Judiciary Committee press release, Sen. Dick Durbin, the committee’s ranking member, said he had received whistleblower information about FBI Director Kash Patel’s use and management of bureau aircraft. Durbin characterized the disclosures as alleging that aircraft decisions affected or delayed high-profile investigations, including the Charlie Kirk killing. As an example, he said the FBI shooting-reconstruction team was asked to fly to Utah to assist with the investigation and process the scene. The release does not provide flight logs, a detailed response timeline, or an independent inspector general finding establishing that Patel’s personal travel delayed that team. It does make a separately worded allegation about the FBI’s response to the Brown University shooting, which should not be conflated with the Kirk investigation. The supportable entry is that a senator publicly disclosed whistleblower allegations and described a requested deployment after Kirk’s killing. It should not state as proven fact that personal aircraft use hampered the Kirk response or multiple emergencies. The FBI’s contemporaneous account says agents arrived at the scene within 16 minutes, a distinct fact that further cautions against overstating the alleged delay.
